chief_complaint: A 4-year-old girl was carried into the A&E department because she had not awoken for 4 hours after a 10-minute generalized seizure that occurred at 5 a.m. that day, following a bad headache and shaking chills the previous evening.
history_of_present_illness: The patient was well until yesterday, when she developed a bad headache in the early afternoon, followed by shaking chills later in the evening. The family believed it was another episode of malaria, common in their village, and planned to take her to a health centre in the morning. She slept restlessly. At 5 a.m. on the day of presentation, the family found her in the midst of a seizure lasting about ten minutes. It took 4 hours for the family to reach A&E, and the child had not awoken since the seizure. There was no recent head trauma, and no other known reason for illness.
exposure_and_epidemiology: The patient resides in rural eastern Uganda during the rainy season, an area of high malaria transmission. Malaria is a common problem in their village, and the family believed this was 'yet another episode of malaria.' People in this region may be frequently bitten by malaria-infected female anopheline mosquitoes.
vitals: Her temperature was 38.7°C (101.7°F), pulse 150 bpm, respiratory rate 36 breath cycles per minute, and blood pressure 98/40 mmHg.
physical_exam: She was deeply comatose with a Blantyre Coma Scale of 1/5. She exhibited no neck stiffness or jaundice and had normal capillary refill. Nasal flaring was present with respirations. Pupils were 2 mm and reactive, and extraocular movements were normal by oculocephalic manoeuvres. Direct ophthalmoscopy showed no papilloedema. With stimulation, there was decerebrate posturing that resolved spontaneously. Cardiac examination revealed a gallop rhythm. Her liver was palpable 2 cm below the right costal margin, and her spleen was 4 cm below the left costal margin.
labs_and_diagnostics: A rapid test for glucose was normal. Initial laboratory results showed a haematocrit of 17.6% (reference range ≥30), a platelet count of 28 ×10^9/L (reference range 150-450), and a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test (RDT) (reference range negative). A lumbar puncture was performed, revealing clear and acellular CSF with normal opening pressure. Blood cultures were taken. Ophthalmoscopy, performed after instilling mydriatic drops, revealed white-centred haemorrhages in both eyes. An EEG showed diffuse slowing but no epileptiform activity.
differential_diagnosis: The primary underlying aetiologies of coma considered include cerebral malaria, acute bacterial meningitis, viral encephalitis, and intoxication (particularly organophosphates). Metabolic abnormalities (hypoglycaemia, renal or hepatic failure) and non-convulsive status epilepticus were also considered as potential primary causes or complications. Although there was no neck stiffness, this finding was deemed less reliable given the deep coma. Hypoglycaemia was ruled out by rapid testing, and a post-ictal state was considered unlikely as 4 hours had passed since the last seizure. Despite a positive malaria RDT, bacterial meningitis remained a possibility, necessitating a lumbar puncture. EEG was considered useful for ruling out non-convulsive status epilepticus.
management_and_clinical_course: Upon arrival, the child received artesunate 2.4 mg/kg IV in the A&E department. She was then admitted to the high-dependency section of the hospital's paediatric unit for frequent monitoring of vital signs and serum glucose. Artesunate was repeated at 12 and 24 hours, and then once daily. Twelve hours after admission, she experienced a short (1 minute) generalized seizure that spontaneously resolved and did not recur. Forty hours after admission, her Blantyre Coma Score had improved to 4/5. The child was discharged home on hospital day five, with a follow-up appointment in the neurology clinic scheduled after 4 weeks.
final_diagnosis: The final diagnosis was retinopathy-positive cerebral malaria, caused by Plasmodium falciparum. This was supported by her presentation in a malaria-endemic region during the rainy season with symptoms suggestive of malaria, a positive malaria rapid diagnostic test, hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia, thrombocytopenia, and critically, the presence of white-centred haemorrhages on ophthalmoscopy, which is a key feature of malarial retinopathy. Her clinical improvement following artesunate treatment further supported the diagnosis.
